title: DUV-guided block-copolymer honeycomb replaces EUV for capacitor array
idea: Worse: add more EUV layers to every shrink. Flip: print only a coarse DUV guide pattern, then let a cylinder-forming high-chi block copolymer self-assemble into the hexagonal lattice that the 6F2 honeycomb storage-node and landing-pad layers already use, tripling density per guide post.
why: Litho/capital (fact 4): removes 2-3 of the 5-7 EUV layers on the array (~8-12% wafer cost). Row/column redundancy absorbs DSA defectivity.

title: Laser interference gratings plus coarse cuts define the whole array
idea: Worse: insist that every array layer needs a $200M scanner and a custom reticle. Flip: expose the purely periodic wordline/bitline layers with maskless two-beam 193 nm immersion interference lithography (a ~$10-20M tool), pitch-split by SAQP, then trim with one low-resolution DUV cut mask. Arrays need periodicity, not arbitrary shapes.
why: Capital intensity: array litho tool cost drops ~10x and array masks shrink to cut layers only.

title: Mass-produced fab modules: build factories like ships, not cathedrals
idea: Worse: build each fab as a bespoke 5-year megaproject. Flip: design a 5k-wafer/month DRAM fab module where tools sit in sealed N2 minienvironments linked by enclosed transport, so no ballroom cleanroom is needed. Build identical modules on an assembly line and drop them onto prepared pads.
why: Capital/time: the cleanroom shell (~25-30% of fab capex) goes away, time to first wafer falls from ~4 to ~1.5 years, and replication drives the module learning curve.

title: Hyperscaler-financed tool SPVs backed by wafer-start futures
idea: Worse: make memory makers carry all depreciation risk so they underinvest at the start of every boom. Flip: hyperscalers buy tradable forward contracts for wafer starts on named tool sets. The contracts collateralize tool-level project finance: each scanner or etcher is owned by an SPV and leased to the fab, off its balance sheet.
why: Capital intensity: depreciation is ~55% of wafer cost; cutting the cost of capital from ~12% to ~6% lowers wafer cost ~10-15% and speeds capacity adds.

title: Ship imperfect dies with burned-in defect maps for OS remapping
idea: Worse: scrap every die that still fails after the repair fuses run out. Flip: sell dies with residual bad rows. An on-die eFuse defect map is read at boot, and the kernel or CXL controller excludes those pages (badblocks for RAM), creating a priced-per-good-GB 'capacity-certified' grade.
why: Throughput/yield: effective yield on large HBM/DDR5 dies rises from ~75% to ~95%, about 15-25% more sellable bits per wafer with no new tools.

title: Freeze the lithography roadmap; scale only by vertical tiers
idea: Worse: retire scanners at every node and buy new ones. Flip: commit to a 10-year litho-frozen DRAM roadmap at a fixed F~16-18 nm, with all density gains from deposition/etch tier stacking, so the scanner fleet fully depreciates and serves 3-4 generations.
why: Litho capital (fact 4): litho is ~25-35% of tool spend, and fully depreciated scanners cut wafer cost ~15-20%. Dep/etch tools are multi-sourced and largely U.S.-made.

title: Metal-assisted chemical etching drills 100:1 capacitor holes wet
idea: Worse: push plasma etch to AR 115:1, with ever slower rates, bowing and twisting. Flip: pattern a perforated catalytic metal mesh and let metal-assisted chemical etching in HF/H2O2 sink the catalyst straight down at room temperature. This gives bow-free holes beyond 100:1 on a wet bench, followed by catalyst strip and clean.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1) plus capital: replaces the costliest high-AR etch chamber-hours with wet benches and makes AR~115 (~1.5x Cs) reachable.

title: Hydrogen backside gas frees etch chucks from Qatari helium
idea: Worse: keep helium backside cooling on every etch and deposition chuck while Qatar's supply is offline. Flip: switch electrostatic chucks to hydrogen backside gas (thermal conductivity ~1.2x helium, already plumbed in fabs) or a compliant CNT thermal pad for clean chambers, and requalify cryo high-AR etch uniformity.
why: Scarce resource: removes a ~30%-Qatar-dependent input from every plasma tool and prevents shortage-driven tool downtime.

title: Periphery from U.S. mature foundries bonded to array-only wafers
idea: Worse: build sense amps and logic in the same costly DRAM process that compromises both. Flip: make array-only wafers in the DRAM fab, buy the periphery wafer (sense amps, decoders, I/O) from a 28/22 nm U.S. foundry, and hybrid-bond the two wafer-to-wafer at sub-micron pitch.
why: Periphery is ~49% of the die (fact 7): DRAM fab bit output per tool rises ~1.6-1.9x, using underused U.S. mature-node capacity.

title: Industry-wide open cell-array mask standard shared by all makers
idea: Worse: every maker pays for proprietary array masks, and entrants must reinvent the cell. Flip: a consortium standardizes one array lattice and pitch and the masks/OPC for its critical array layers, licensed royalty-free. Vendors differentiate only in periphery, materials and capacitors.
why: Capital/entry barrier: entrants skip ~$1-2B of array integration R&D, and mask and OPC learning is pooled, enabling U.S. second sources.

title: Double-sided wafers: native two-high stacks on both faces
idea: Worse: use only one face of every expensive crystal wafer. Flip: run FEOL on both faces in edge-gripped double-sided tools. Furnace anneals and blanket depositions treat both faces in one pass, while litho alternates sides. TSVs then link the faces into a native two-high die stack without any bonding step.
why: Bits per wafer start ~1.8x with shared thermal/deposition steps; crucible-limited substrate use per bit roughly halves; HBM gets one bond layer free.

title: Federated defect-image library compresses new-fab yield ramps
idea: Worse: every new fab learns its defects alone over 2-3 years. Flip: entrants and toolmakers feed inline SEM/optical defect images and parametric fails into a standardized defect taxonomy. Classifiers train federated (data never leaves each fab) and ship root-cause models and recipe corrections to new lines on day one.
why: Capital: ramp months burn depreciation (~55% of wafer cost); cutting the ramp from ~24 to ~10 months saves ~$1B+ per new fab.

title: Restart mothballed 2x-nm lines for stacked capacity-tier memory
idea: Worse: insist that all supply comes from leading-node fabs. Flip: buy idle, fully depreciated 300 mm lines (old DRAM, logic or NAND) and run a simplified 25-30 nm, zero-EUV DRAM. Stack 8-16 dies into CXL far-memory modules, where $/GB matters more than density per die.
why: Capital intensity: near-zero depreciation keeps $/bit competitive despite ~3-4x larger cells; online in 12-18 months on U.S. soil.

title: Rotary spatial ALD conveyor for capacitor dielectric stacks
idea: Worse: deposit ZrO2/Al2O3/ZrO2 capacitor stacks by slow pulse-purge temporal ALD. Flip: carry wafers on a rotating platen under gas-curtain-separated precursor zones (spatial ALD from solar passivation), so each revolution is one cycle at ~10x throughput and higher precursor utilization.
why: Throughput/capital: capacitor dielectric/electrode tool count falls ~60-80% and Zr/Hf precursor use drops.

title: Sideways cell: film thickness, not lithography, sets every dimension
idea: Worse: make every critical dimension depend on optical resolution. Flip: rotate the access transistor 90 degrees so gate length, channel thickness and capacitor dielectric are ALD films grown on the sidewalls of coarse 80 nm DUV trenches. Litho only cuts trenches; Angstrom-precise deposition 'prints' the sub-10 nm features.
why: Litho-bound scaling (fact 4): scaling continues by deposition without EUV, toward ~4F2 at relaxed F.

title: Open-hardware process chambers built by U.S. machine shops
idea: Worse: depend on a handful of tool vendors with 18-month lead times. Flip: fund open-source reference designs for ALD, etch and furnace modules with standard SEMI interfaces and open controllers. A national lab qualifies each once; regional machine shops then build and service them, like certified aircraft parts.
why: Tool capex (~70-80% of fab cost): targets ~40-50% cheaper non-litho tools with ~6-month lead times and U.S. manufacturing.

title: Counter-cyclical strategic DRAM reserve keeps fabs fully utilized
idea: Worse: let downturns idle fabs and freeze capex, so the next shortage is deeper. Flip: a government/hyperscaler reserve buys known-good DRAM wafers at a floor price during gluts, stores them in dry nitrogen vaults, and releases them during spikes, like a petroleum reserve for bits.
why: Capital intensity: guaranteed utilization lowers the risk premium on fab capex, keeps investment steady and damps 4x price swings.

title: Area-selective deposition grows landing pads without a mask
idea: Worse: add a litho-plus-etch layer with tight overlay for every contact and landing pad. Flip: SAM inhibitors block nucleation on dielectric, so ALD/CVD metal grows only on the exposed plug tops. This builds self-aligned landing pads and contacts and removes 2-3 critical litho layers along with their overlay budgets.
why: Masks/EUV (fact 4): 2-3 fewer critical layers (~5-8% wafer cost) and higher overlay-limited yield.

title: Reusable porous-silicon seed wafers slash crucible-quartz demand
idea: Worse: consume one Czochralski crystal slice, and its share of a Spruce Pine crucible, per wafer. Flip: grow a 20-50 um epitaxial device layer on a porous-Si release layer, transfer it to a cheap carrier or the bonded periphery wafer, and reuse the seed wafer 20-50 times.
why: Scarce resource: high-purity quartz crucible use per wafer falls 90%+ and substrate cost drops.

title: Probe-less wafer test: on-die BIST powered and read optically
idea: Worse: test every die on multimillion-dollar ATE with slow probe-card touchdowns. Flip: put a tiny photovoltaic cell and an LED/photodiode link on every die. Flood-illuminate the wafer so all dies self-test with on-die BIST at once and report pass/fail and repair maps optically in parallel.
why: Test is ~10-15% of DRAM cost; massively parallel optical test cuts tester capex and test time ~5-10x.

title: Pure-play DRAM foundry with open PDK for fabless designers
idea: Worse: keep the DRAM process locked inside three IDMs. Flip: a DRAM foundry offers an array PDK (cell, capacitor, sense-amp macros) and multi-project wafers, so fabless startups and hyperscalers can tape out custom PIM, wide-I/O or CXL-native DRAM.
why: Capital: spreads utilization over many customers, unlocks designs that do DRAM's job with fewer bits, and opens a U.S. entry path.

title: Undiced wafer-scale DRAM panels for rack memory pools
idea: Worse: dice, package and test thousands of dies, each losing scribe and edge area. Flip: keep the whole wafer as one memory, with reticle-stitched interconnect and die/row-level redundancy routing. Mount it directly in a rack memory appliance behind a wafer-level CXL fabric.
why: Packaging, test and scribe are ~15-25% of cost; redundancy turns defects into lost capacity, not scrap; ~20% lower $/GB for pooled memory.

title: Colorado molybdenum replaces Chinese tungsten in buried wordlines
idea: Worse: keep 80%-China tungsten in every buried wordline, contact and plug. Flip: switch to fluorine-free, barrierless Mo CVD sourced from U.S. Climax/Henderson mines; Mo has lower resistivity than W at thin dimensions.
why: Scarce-resource chokepoint removed; ~20-30% lower wordline RC also permits thinner, denser lines.

title: Idle Gen-8.5 display fabs make glass-panel memory
idea: Worse: limit DRAM to round 300 mm wafers while LCD fabs sit idle. Flip: convert surplus Gen-8.5 display lines (2.2x2.5 m glass, ~70x a wafer's area) to make oxide-TFT gain-cell memory panels with their existing steppers and sputter/PECVD tools, then dice them into tiles for capacity-tier modules.
why: Capital: ~$1-2B conversion versus $15B+ for a new fab; panel area offsets ~10-20x lower density; no crucible quartz, no EUV.

title: Roll-to-roll memory tape on stainless steel foil
idea: Worse: process memory one rigid wafer at a time through vacuum load locks. Flip: run 30 um stainless-steel foil, planarized with spin-on glass, through roll-to-roll UV nanoimprint, atmospheric deposition and sputter zones to make cell layers continuously, then cut and stack the tape into blocks.
why: Throughput/capital: continuous web at meters/min, tool cost per m2 ~10-50x below wafer fabs, abundant U.S.-made steel.

title: Sapphire miscut step-bunches template sub-10nm wordlines without lithography
idea: Worse: print every line with a photon. Flip: anneal vicinal c-plane sapphire until its atomic steps bunch into a periodic 8-20 nm terrace grating, then decorate the step edges by step-flow selective nucleation of metal or oxide semiconductor. Parallel wordlines then form across the whole substrate.
why: Litho (fact 4): a sub-EUV-pitch wordline layer at zero mask cost, on sapphire grown without quartz crucibles.

title: Anodic alumina pores on glass grow vertical access transistors
idea: Worse: pattern every vertical transistor with EUV contact holes. Flip: sputter aluminum on glass and anodize it into self-ordered 20-40 nm hexagonal pores. Fill the pores with ALD oxide-semiconductor channels wrapped by an ALD gate, giving vertical gate-all-around 4F2 access transistors with no transistor-level lithography.
why: Masks/EUV: removes the critical hole layer and reaches 4F2 density with low-capex anodization baths on glass.

title: MLCC tape-casting lines build high-k capacitor substrates
idea: Worse: fight the 5 fF wall with ever-deeper etched holes. Flip: use the multilayer-ceramic-capacitor industry's tape-cast, co-fired BaTiO3 (k>1000) as the substrate: hundreds of sub-um layers with one via electrode per cell, topped by thin-film access transistors. Charge comes from k, not aspect ratio.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1 needs k~70): k in the thousands, made on low-capex, high-volume MLCC lines.

title: Repurpose idle SiC power fabs for ultra-low-leakage DRAM
idea: Worse: let EV-slowdown SiC fabs idle while DRAM is scarce. Flip: build 1T1C DRAM on 150/200 mm 4H-SiC wafers in existing SiC fabs. The 3.2 eV bandgap cuts generation leakage by orders of magnitude (1990s SiC DRAM cells held charge for hours), so refresh nearly vanishes, and the lower density is accepted for capacity tiers.
why: Refresh (fact 3) plus capital: reuses sunk U.S. SiC capacity (NC, NY) and needs no Si crucibles.

title: Thermally drawn multimaterial fibers woven into memory fabric
idea: Worse: build memory only by stacking films on flat plates. Flip: draw a macroscopic metal/semiconductor/insulator preform into kilometers of fiber whose cross-section holds a storage capacitor and an access junction. Weave orthogonal fibers into a crossbar fabric so every crossing is an addressable cell.
why: Capital: fiber towers cost ~$1M and run km/hour with no lithography, a speculative path to cheap bulk capacity.

title: Plywood DRAM: laser-lifted polyimide tiers laminated into stacks
idea: Worse: grow 26+ tiers sequentially on one substrate, so one bad tier scraps them all. Flip: fabricate each tier in parallel on polyimide over a reusable glass carrier, test it, laser-lift-off the good ones with OLED LLO tools, and laminate 32 known-good tiers with self-aligned through-tier vias.
why: 3D DRAM (fact 2): known-good-tier stacking breaks the compounded-yield trap and reuses idle OLED tools.

title: Electrohydrodynamic jet printing makes mask-free personalization layers on glass
idea: Worse: buy a new mask set for every memory variant. Flip: on standard glass-panel memory arrays, write the variable layers (wordline strapping, redundancy routing, I/O fan-out) with multi-nozzle e-jet printing of nanoparticle inks at ~100 nm, so one array panel serves many products.
why: Masks/capital: zero mask cost per variant makes low-volume specialty memory viable.

title: Silicon-on-sapphire cells eliminate substrate junction leakage tail
idea: Worse: keep the storage-node junction in a bulk crystal whose defects create the 13 fA tail. Flip: put thin epitaxial Si on Kyropoulos sapphire, so the node has no substrate junction and leaks only through the channel. Sapphire boules use molybdenum crucibles, not high-purity quartz.
why: Refresh (fact 3): removes the junction/GIDL tail for ~10x retention, on a substrate independent of Spruce Pine.

title: Tunnel-etched electrolytic-capacitor aluminum foil becomes DRAM capacitor plate
idea: Worse: plasma-etch every capacitor hole into hard crystal. Flip: borrow the electrolytic-capacitor industry's DC tunnel etching, which in seconds drills straight crystallographic <100> tunnels above 50:1 into Al foil. Seed the tunnel sites with a pattern, coat them with ALD high-k and a top electrode, and use the foil itself as the common plate.
why: Capacitor wall plus capital: wet electrochemical etch at $/m2 cost replaces high-AR plasma etchers.

title: Drawn nanochannel glass gives billion-hole capacitor templates
idea: Worse: create capacitor holes one etch step at a time at AR 75:1. Flip: stack and redraw glass rods with etchable cores again and again (nanochannel glass has reached ~30 nm channels) into plates of uniform hexagonal channels beyond 100:1. Etch out the cores, ALD the electrodes and dielectric, and bond a thin-film transistor layer on top.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): AR above 100 comes free from drawing, with no plasma etch; glass is U.S.-made.

title: Remote epitaxy through graphene lets one template seed hundreds of tiers
idea: Worse: consume a fresh single-crystal substrate for every device layer. Flip: grow single-crystal oxide or III-N films through a graphene interlayer on a reusable sapphire/GaN template, peel each membrane off with a Ni stressor, and stack the membranes as 3D memory tiers. The template is reused for every peel.
why: 3D DRAM (fact 2): crystalline tiers without Si/SiGe epi stacks, with substrate cost amortized ~100x.

title: Wafer-scale MoS2 epitaxy on sapphire for stackable access transistors
idea: Worse: insist that the access transistor be bulk crystalline silicon. Flip: grow single-crystal monolayer MoS2 by MOCVD on step-engineered sapphire and stack transistor layers monolithically at <400 C. The 1.8 eV gap and 0.7 nm body give sub-fA off-current and atomically thin tiers.
why: 3D DRAM tier pitch shrinks ~5x versus Si/SiGe epi, and the leakage tail falls (fact 3).

title: CVD diamond substrates remove the thermal ceiling on stacking
idea: Worse: stack memory on a substrate that traps heat, so retention collapses and refresh doubles above 85 C. Flip: build tiers on thin polycrystalline CVD diamond plates (~1500 W/mK) that hold stacked arrays near coolant temperature. Leakage roughly halves for each ~10 C of cooling, so stacks of 16-24 tiers stay viable.
why: Refresh (fact 3) and HBM thermals: ~2-4x retention and more tiers per stack; diamond is grown from methane in U.S. reactors.

title: Cleaved mica substrates give atomic flatness without CMP
idea: Worse: add dozens of CMP steps and ceria slurry to flatten each layer. Flip: start on cleaved muscovite mica, atomically flat over cm2. Grow oxide-semiconductor and high-k films by van der Waals epitaxy, and keep later tiers flat by vdW-bonded transfer instead of polishing.
why: Process steps: removes ~10-20% of CMP steps and their ceria consumables, on an abundant U.S.-mined substrate.

title: Origami memory: fold a low-resolution sheet into 3D density
idea: Worse: chase density by shrinking features with ever costlier lithography. Flip: pattern a large memory sheet on polyimide at relaxed 100+ nm rules with stress-engineered SiN/metal hinge lines, then release it and fold it accordion-style into 50-100 layers. Interconnect runs across the hinges instead of through vias.
why: Litho/capital: density by folding instead of shrinking, with DUV-only tools.

title: Strain-driven rolled-up nanomembrane capacitors on glass
idea: Worse: build capacitors as ever-taller, fragile pillars. Flip: deposit a pre-strained bilayer carrying an electrode/high-k/electrode stack on a sacrificial layer over glass, then release it so it self-rolls into a Swiss-roll capacitor about 10 windings deep. This multiplies plate area per footprint without deep etching.
why: Capacitor charge wall: effective AR above 100 by rolling, with no high-AR etch and no pattern collapse.

title: Glass-core HBM base replaces silicon interposer and TSV die
idea: Worse: spend 3x wafer area per bit and TSV yield losses on silicon interposers. Flip: build HBM base routing and through-vias in glass-core panels (laser-modified, wet-etched TGVs at ~10 um pitch) on 510x515 mm panel lines, and hybrid-bond the DRAM dies to the glass.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): frees the silicon interposer/base area at ~3-5x lower panel cost per area, with U.S. glass suppliers.

title: Substrate-agnostic memory qualification standard unlocks non-silicon suppliers
idea: Worse: write qualification specs that implicitly assume bulk-Si dies and block every alternative. Flip: create a JEDEC/OCP 'memory tile' standard defined only by electrical, thermal and reliability behavior plus a tile form factor, with funded shared qualification labs, so glass, SiC or ceramic memory is qualified once and bought widely.
why: Strategy: removes the ~2-3-year qualification barrier for non-Si capacity and attracts new capital.

title: Dieless memory: deposit arrays directly on the package substrate
idea: Worse: make a die on one substrate, dice it, and bond it onto another (the package). Flip: build low-temperature oxide-TFT memory arrays directly on the glass-core package panel that carries the processor. The result has no die, dicing, bonding or separate test insertion, with memory millimeters from compute.
why: Packaging capital plus data movement (fact 5): die and assembly costs vanish, and short wires cut pJ/bit.

title: Blu-ray replication lines injection-mold nanostructured capacitor templates
idea: Worse: let idle optical-disc factories rot while capacitor etch bottlenecks fabs. Flip: injection-mold high-temperature PEI/PEEK substrates from a nickel stamper carrying ~100 nm pit arrays at ~3 s per part. ALD low-temperature electrodes and high-k into the pits, then laminate an oxide-TFT layer on top.
why: Capital: stamper replication costs ~cents per part versus EUV plus high-AR etch, on reused disc lines.

title: Online CVD on hot float-glass ribbon deposits memory blanket layers
idea: Worse: deposit every blanket film in a $5M vacuum chamber, one substrate at a time. Flip: as float glass leaves the tin bath at ~600 C, apply atmospheric online CVD (already used for pyrolytic low-E coatings) to lay down barrier, bottom-electrode and oxide-semiconductor blanket layers at kilometers per day, then cut panels for patterning.
why: Throughput/capital: blanket deposition cost per m2 ~100x lower, using existing U.S. float lines.
